extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, systematists, geologists, and biologists interested in evolution and classification
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for delimiting species, constructing classifications as genealogies, and inferring historical processes (migration, time, ancestry) from morphology, embryology, and the fossil record. Also outlines priorities for future research into variation and the components any evolutionary explanation should address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species delimitation: constancy and distinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematists must decide whether any form "be sufficiently constant and distinct from other forms, to be capable of definition; and if definable, whether the differences be sufficiently important to deserve a specific name."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on small differences or on the mere absence/presence of intermediate forms; instead weigh whether a form is sufficiently constant and distinct to be definable and whether differences merit specific rank. The author predicts systematists will shift emphasis to the actual amount of difference between forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish species from well-marked varieties by intermediate gradations
rubrics_metrics.description: "The only distinction between species and well-marked varieties is, that the latter are known, or believed, to be connected at the present day by intermediate gradations, whereas species were formerly thus connected."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether two forms are species or varieties, examine evidence for intermediate gradations now versus in the past; present continuities indicate varieties, historical continuity (now broken) indicates species. This changes emphasis from absolutes to historical connectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value the actual amount of difference between forms
rubrics_metrics.description: We shall be led "to weigh more carefully and to value higher the actual amount of difference between them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In classification and naming decisions, prioritize quantitative/qualitative magnitude of difference over mere presence of some distinguishing trait; small but consistent differences may be less important if intermediate gradations exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifications should aim to be genealogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Our classifications "will come to be, as far as they can be so made, genealogies; and will then truly give what may be called the plan of creation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer classificatory schemes that represent lines of descent. When constructing classifications, use characters that reflect inheritance and shared ancestry rather than only convenience-based groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudimentary organs as evidence of ancestral structures
rubrics_metrics.description: "Rudimentary organs will speak infallibly with respect to the nature of long-lost structures."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat vestigial/rudimentary structures as strong evidence of former, fully-developed organs in ancestors; use them as diagnostic characters when inferring phylogenetic history and lost structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use embryological characters to infer prototypes and relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Embryology "will reveal to us the structure, in some degree obscured, of the prototypes of each great class."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate embryological development and succession of embryonic characters into assessments of relationships and ancestral states; embryological similarity can indicate common prototypes even when adult forms differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret fossiliferous formations as episodic and the geological record as imperfect
rubrics_metrics.description: The crust of the earth "must not be looked at as a well-filled museum, but as a poor collection made at hazard and at rare intervals." "The accumulation of each great fossiliferous formation will be recognised as having depended on an unusual concurrence of circumstances, and the blank intervals between the successive stages as having been of vast duration."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using the fossil record, allow for large gaps, episodic deposition, and preservation bias. Do not assume continuous deposition or completeness; be cautious in drawing strict sequential inferences from apparent absences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious correlating formations with few identical species
rubrics_metrics.description: We must "be cautious in attempting to correlate as strictly contemporaneous two formations, which include few identical species, by the general succession of their forms of life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid strict temporal correlation of geographically separated formations when they share few identical species; prefer multiple lines of evidence (stratigraphy, geology, tectonics) and acknowledge uncertainty where faunal/floral overlap is sparse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of organic change as a proxy for lapse of time (with caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of organic change in the fossils of consecutive formations "probably serves as a fair measure of the lapse of actual time," but "we must not overrate the accuracy of organic change as a measure of time" because groups may remain unchanged or be modified by migration and competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the degree of faunal/floral change between successive formations as one rough indicator of elapsed time, but apply caution: differential rates of change, stasis, migration, and ecological factors can decouple measured change from absolute time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer secondary causes and slow, continuous processes over miraculous explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: "The production and extinction of the past and present inhabitants of the world should have been due to secondary causes, like those determining the birth and death of the individual... the ordinary succession by generation has never once been broken, and that no cataclysm has desolated the whole world."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating historical explanations, favor hypotheses invoking continuous, observable processes (variation, selection, competition, migration) rather than one-off miraculous or catastrophic events unless strong evidence demands them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research priorities: study variation, correlation, and domestication to understand laws of change
rubrics_metrics.description: A grand field for inquiry: "the causes and laws of variation, on correlation of growth, on the effects of use and disuse, on the direct action of external conditions, and so forth. The study of domestic productions will rise immensely in value."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize empirical research on variation (including domestic varieties), correlation of traits, effects of use/disuse, and environmental action as sources of evidence for mechanisms of change. Domestic breeding experiments and studies of cultivated varieties are especially valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components any account of organic origins must address (summary of mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws taken in the largest sense are: Growth with Reproduction; Inheritance; Variability from external conditions and use/disuse; A Ratio of Increase leading to a Struggle for Life; Natural Selection entailing Divergence of Character and Extinction of less-improved forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any satisfactory explanatory framework for the origin of species should explicitly consider and account for: reproduction and growth, inheritance, sources of variability, population increase and competition (struggle for life), selection acting on variation, divergence of character, and extinction. Use these components as criteria when assessing evolutionary explanations.
